{{Short description|Theorem in statistics}}
{{About|the theorem in mathematical statistics|the theorem in real analysis|extreme value theorem}}

In [[mathematical statistics]], the '''Fisher–Tippett–Gnedenko theorem''' (also the '''Fisher–Tippett theorem''' or the '''extreme value theorem''') is a general result in [[extreme value theory]] regarding [[asymptotic distribution]] of extreme [[order statistic]]s. The maximum of a sample of [[iid]] [[random variable]]s after proper renormalization can only [[converges in distribution|converge in distribution]] to one of three possible [[location-scale family|distribution families]]: the [[Gumbel distribution]], the [[Fréchet distribution]], or the [[Weibull distribution]]. Credit for the extreme value theorem and its convergence details are given to [[Fréchet]] (1927),<ref>{{cite journal | last = Fréchet | first = M. | year = 1927 | title = Sur la loi de probabilité de l'écart maximum | journal = Annales de la Société Polonaise de Mathématique | volume = 6 | issue = 1 | pages = 93–116 }}</ref> [[Ronald Fisher|Fisher]] and  [[Leonard Henry Caleb Tippett|Tippett]] (1928),<ref>{{cite journal
| last1 = Fisher | first1 = R. A. | authorlink1=Ronald Fisher
| last2 = Tippett | first2 = L. H. C. | authorlink2=Leonard Henry Caleb Tippett
| date = 1928
| title = Limiting forms of the frequency distribution of the largest and smallest member of a sample
| journal = [[Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society]]
| volume = 24
| issue = 2
| pages = 180–190
| doi=10.1017/s0305004100015681 | bibcode = 1928PCPS...24..180F | s2cid = 123125823}}</ref> [[Richard von Mises|von Mises]] (1936),<ref name=mises/><ref name=falk/> and [[Gnedenko]] (1943).<ref name=gnedenko>{{cite journal | last1 = Gnedenko | first1 = B.V. | year = 1943 | title = Sur la distribution limite du terme maximum d'une serie aleatoire | journal = [[Annals of Mathematics]] | volume = 44 | issue = 3| pages = 423–453 | doi=10.2307/1968974| jstor = 1968974 }}</ref>

The role of the extremal types theorem for maxima is similar to that of [[central limit theorem]] for averages, except that the central limit theorem applies to the average of a sample from any distribution with finite variance, while the Fisher–Tippet–Gnedenko theorem only states that ''if'' the distribution of a normalized maximum converges, ''then'' the limit has to be one of a particular class of distributions. It does not state that the distribution of the normalized maximum does converge.

A formal statement can be found in the Chapman & Hall/CRC ''Handbook of Statistics of Extremes''.<ref>
{{cite book
 |last1=de Carvalho |first1=M.
 |last2=Huser |first2=R.
 |last3=Naveau |first3=P.
 |last4=Reich |first4=B. J.
 |date=2026
 |title=Handbook of Statistics of Extremes
 |publisher=Chapman & Hall/CRC
 |location=Boca Raton, FL
 |isbn= 978-1-0325-1980-7
 |url = https://extremestats.github.io/Handbook
}} 
</ref>

==Statement==

Let <math>X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n</math> be an {{mvar|n}}-sized sample of [[independent and identically-distributed random variables]], each of whose [[cumulative distribution function]] is <math>F</math>. Suppose that there exist two sequences of real numbers <math>a_n > 0</math> and <math>b_n \in \mathbb{R}</math> such that the following limits converge to a non-[[degenerate distribution]] function:

:<math> \lim_{n \to \infty} \mathbb{P}\left( \frac{\max\{X_1, \dots, X_n\} - b_n}{ a_n } \leq x \right) = G(x) ,</math>
or equivalently:

:<math> \lim_{n \to \infty}\bigl(F(a_n x + b_n)\bigr)^n = G(x) .</math>

In such circumstances, the limiting function <math>G</math> is the cumulative distribution function of a  distribution belonging to either the [[Gumbel distribution|Gumbel]], the [[Fréchet distribution|Fréchet]], or the [[Weibull distribution|Weibull]] [[location-scale family|distribution family]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Mood |first=A.M. |year=1950 |title=Introduction to the theory of statistics |publisher=McGraw-Hill |location=New York, NY |chapter= 5. Order Statistics | pages= 251–270}}</ref>

In other words, if the limit above converges, then up to a linear change of coordinates <math>G(x)</math> will assume either the form:<ref name=haan>{{cite book |last1=Haan |first1=Laurens |last2=Ferreira |first2=Ana |year=2007 |title=Extreme Value Theory: An introduction |publisher=Springer}}</ref>

:<math> G_\gamma(x) = \exp\big( \!-( 1 + \gamma x )^{-1 / \gamma }\big) \quad \text{for } \gamma \ne 0 ,</math>

with the non-zero parameter <math>\gamma</math> also satisfying <math>1 + \gamma x > 0</math> for every <math>x</math> value supported by <math>F</math> (for all values <math>x</math> for which <math>F(x) \ne 0</math>).{{clarify|date=July 2024|reason=Needs a clearer formula / definition / relation for key factor γ . What's given, 1 + γ x > 0, is too vague.}} Otherwise it has the form:

: <math> G_0(x) = \exp\bigl(\!-\exp(-x)\bigr) \quad \text{for } \gamma = 0 .</math>

This is the cumulative distribution function of the [[generalized extreme value distribution]] (GEV) with extreme value index <math>\gamma</math>. The GEV distribution groups the Gumbel, Fréchet, and Weibull distributions into a single composite form.

==Conditions of convergence==

The Fisher–Tippett–Gnedenko theorem is a statement about the convergence of the limiting distribution <math>G(x)</math>, above. The study of conditions for convergence of <math>G</math> to particular cases of the generalized extreme value distribution began with Mises (1936)<ref name='mises'>{{cite journal |last=von&nbsp;Mises |first=R. |author-link=Richard von Mises |year=1936 |title=La distribution de la plus grande de {{mvar|n}} valeurs |lang=fr |trans-title=The distribution of the largest of {{mvar|n}} values |journal=Rev. Math. Union Interbalcanique |series=1 |pages=141–160}}</ref><ref name=gnedenko/><ref name=falk>{{cite journal |author1=Falk, Michael |author2=Marohn, Frank |title=von Mises conditions revisited |journal=The Annals of Probability |year=1993 |pages=1310–1328}}</ref> and was further developed by Gnedenko (1943).<ref name=gnedenko/>

Let <math>F</math> be the distribution function of <math>X</math>, and <math>X_1, \dots, X_n</math> be some [[independent and identically distributed random variables|i.i.d.]] sample thereof. Also let <math>x_\mathsf{max}</math> be the population maximum: <math>x_\mathsf{max} \equiv \sup \{x \mid F(x) < 1\}</math>.

Then the limiting distribution of the normalized sample maximum, given by <math>G</math> above, will then be one of the following three types:<ref name=haan/>

* '''[[Fréchet distribution]]''' (<math>\gamma > 0</math>): For strictly positive <math>\gamma > 0</math>, the limiting distribution converges if and only if <math>x_\mathsf{max} = \infty</math> and
:: <math>\lim_{t \rightarrow \infty} \frac{1 - F(ut)}{ 1 - F(t) } = u^{-1/\gamma }\ </math> for all <math>u > 0</math>.
: In this case, possible sequences that will satisfy the theorem conditions are <math>b_n = 0</math> and <math>a_n = F^{-1} \! \left( 1-\tfrac{1}{n} \right)</math>. Strictly positive  <math>\gamma</math> corresponds to what is called a ''[[heavy tail]]ed'' distribution.
* '''[[Gumbel distribution]]''' (<math>\gamma = 0</math>): For trivial <math>\gamma = 0</math>, and with <math>x_\mathsf{max}</math> either finite or infinite, the limiting distribution converges if and only if
::<math>\lim_{t \rightarrow x_\mathsf{max} } \frac{ 1 - F(t + u \, \tilde{g}(t)) }{ 1 - F(t) } = \mathrm{e}^{-u}</math> for all <math>u > 0</math> with <math>\tilde{g}(t) \equiv \frac{\int_{t}^{ x_\mathsf{max} }\bigl(1 - F(s)\bigr)\, \mathrm{d}s }{ 1 - F(t) }</math>.
: Possible sequences here are <math>b_n = F^{-1} \left(\ 1 - \tfrac{1}{n}\right)</math> and <math>a_n = \tilde{g}\bigl( F^{-1} \! \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{n}\right)\bigr)</math>.
* '''[[Weibull distribution]]''' (<math>\gamma < 0</math>): For strictly negative <math>\gamma < 0</math>, the limiting distribution converges if and only if <math> x_\mathsf{max} < \infty</math> (is finite) and
:: <math>\lim_{t \rightarrow 0^+} \frac{ 1 - F(x_\mathsf{max} - ut)}{ 1 - F(x_\mathsf{max} - t) } = u^{-1/\gamma}</math> for all <math>u > 0</math>.
: Note that for this case the exponential term <math>-1/\gamma</math> is strictly positive, since <math>\gamma</math> is strictly negative.
: Possible sequences here are <math>b_n = x_\mathsf{max}</math> and <math>a_n = x_\mathsf{max} - F^{-1} \! \left( 1 - \tfrac{1}{n}\right)</math>.

Note that the second formula (the Gumbel distribution) is the limit of the first (the Fréchet distribution) as <math>\gamma</math> goes to zero.

==Examples==
{{Unreferenced section|date=April 2023}}

===Fréchet distribution===
The [[Cauchy distribution]]'s density function is:

:<math>f(x) = \frac{ 1 }{\ \pi(1 + x^2) \ }\ ,</math>

and its cumulative distribution function is:

:<math> F(x) = \frac{\ 1\ }{ 2 } + \frac{1}{\ \pi\ } \arctan\left( \frac{ x }{\ \pi\ } \right) ~.</math>

A little bit of calculus show that the right tail's cumulative distribution <math>\ 1 - F(x)\ </math> is [[asymptotic]] to <math>\ \frac{ 1 }{\ x\ }\ ,</math> or

:<math> \ln F(x) \rightarrow \frac{-1~}{\ x\ } \quad \mathsf{~ as ~} \quad x \rightarrow \infty \ ,</math><!-- fixed notation err: used "sim" for (asymptoticly) "approx". -->

so we have

:<math> \ln \left(\ F(x)^n\ \right) = n\ \ln F(x) \sim \frac{ -n~~ }{ x } ~.</math>

Thus we have

:<math> F(x)^n \approx \exp \left( \frac{ -n~~ }{ x } \right) </math>

and letting <math>\ u \equiv \frac{ x }{\ n\ } - 1\ </math> (and skipping some explanation)

:<math> \lim_{n \to \infty}\Bigl(\ F\bigl(\ n\ (u + 1)\ \bigr)^n\ \Bigr) = \exp\left( \tfrac{-1~}{\ 1 + u \ } \right) = G_1(u)\ </math>

for any <math>\ u ~.</math>

===Gumbel distribution===
Let us take the [[normal distribution]] with cumulative distribution function

:<math>F(x) = \frac{1}{2} \operatorname{erfc}\left( \frac{-x~}{\ \sqrt{2\ }\ } \right) ~.</math>

We have

:<math>\ln F(x)\ \rightarrow\ - \frac{\ \exp\left( -\tfrac{1}{2} x^2 \right)\ }{ \sqrt{2\pi\ }\ x } \qquad \mathsf{~ as ~} \qquad x\ \rightarrow\ \infty </math><!-- fixed notation err: used "sim" for (asymptoticly) "approx". -->

and thus

:<math> \ln \left(\ F(x)^n\ \right) = n \ln F(x)\ \rightarrow\ -\frac{\ n \exp\left( -\tfrac{1}{2} x^2 \right)\ }{ \sqrt{2 \pi\ }\ x } \qquad \mathsf{~ as ~} \qquad x\ \rightarrow\ \infty ~.</math><!-- fixed notation err: used "sim" for (asymptoticly) "approx". -->

Hence we have

:<math> F(x)^n \approx \exp \left( -\ \frac{\ n\ \exp\left( -\tfrac{1}{2} x^2 \right)\ }{\ \sqrt{2\pi\ }\ x\ } \right) ~.</math>

If we define <math>\ c_n\ </math> as the value that exactly satisfies

:<math> \frac{\ n \exp\left( -\ \tfrac{1}{2} c_n^2 \right)\ }{\ \sqrt{2\pi\ }\ c_n\ } = 1\ ,</math>

then for <math>\ x \approx c_n\ ,</math> we find that

:<math>\frac{\ n\ \exp \left( -\ \tfrac{1}{2} x^2 \right)\ }{ \sqrt{2\pi\ }\ x } \approx \exp\left(\ c_n\ ( c_n - x )\ \right) ~.</math>

As <math>\ n\ </math> increases, this becomes a good approximation for a wider and wider range of <math>\ c_n\ ( c_n - x )\ </math> so letting <math>\ u \equiv c_n\ ( x - c_n)\ </math> we find that

:<math>\lim_{n \to \infty}\biggl(\ F\left( \tfrac{u}{~ c_n\ } + c_n \right)^n\ \biggr) = \exp\! \Bigl( -\exp(-u) \Bigr) = G_0(u) ~.</math>

Equivalently, 

:<math>\lim_{n \to \infty} \mathbb{P}\ \Biggl( \frac{\ \max \{ X_1,\ \ldots,\ X_n \} - c_n\ }{ \left( \frac{1}{~ c_n\ } \right) } \leq u \Biggr) = \exp\! \Bigl( -\exp(-u) \Bigr) = G_0(u) ~.</math>

With this result, we see retrospectively that we need <math>\ \ln c_n \approx \frac{\ \ln\ln n\ }{ 2 }\ </math> and then

:<math> c_n \approx \sqrt{ 2\ln n\ }\ ,</math>

so the maximum is expected to climb toward infinity ever more slowly.

===Weibull distribution===
We may take the simplest example, a uniform distribution between {{math|0}} and {{math|1}}, with cumulative distribution function

:<math> F(x) = x\ </math> for any  {{mvar|x}}  value from  {{math|0}}  to  {{math|1}}&nbsp;.

For values of <math>\ x\ \rightarrow\ 1\ </math> we have

:<math>\ln\Bigl(\ F(x)^n\ \Bigr) = n\ \ln F(x)\ \rightarrow\  n\ (\ 1 - x\ ) ~.</math><!-- fixed notation err: used "sim" for (asymptoticly) "approx". -->

So for <math>\ x \approx 1\ </math> we have

:<math>\ F(x)^n \approx \exp(\ n - n\ x\ ) ~.</math>

Let <math>\ u \equiv 1 + n\ (\ 1 - x\ )\ </math> and get

:<math> \lim_{n \to \infty} \Bigl(\ F\! \left( \tfrac{\ u\ }{n} + 1 - \tfrac{\ 1\ }{ n } \right)\ \Bigr)^n = \exp\! \bigl(\ -(1 - u)\ \bigr) = G_{-1}(u) ~.</math>

Close examination of that limit shows that the expected maximum approaches  {{math|1}}  in inverse proportion to  {{mvar|n}}&nbsp;.
